english: Please take me to this address.
usage: 존댓말 — what you say to a taxi driver while showing your phone screen
반말 — only to a friend driving, never to a real taxi driver
Could you take me to this address, please?
More formal/softer — adds politeness when handing over a written address
Natural extension — checking the driver can find it before setting off
examples: 기사님, 이 주소로 가 주세요.
Driver, please take me to this address.
기사님 is the standard polite way to address a taxi driver
이 주소로 가 주세요. 내비에 찍어 주시면 돼요.
Please go to this address. You can just put it in the GPS.
내비 = navigation/GPS; offering to let the driver enter it
이 주소로 가 주세요. 영어로 되어 있는데 제가 읽어 드릴게요.
Please take me to this address. It's in English, but I'll read it for you.
Real situation when your address is only in English on a booking app
nuance: This is the opening line you say to a taxi driver as you get in and show or read an address, customer-to-driver, and the politeness is plain 존댓말 (가 주세요 = 'please go'), which is exactly right for any stranger providing a service. To sound warmer or more formal add 기사님 ('driver, sir/ma'am') at the front and use 가 주시겠어요? The 반말 form 가 줘 is only for a friend who happens to be driving you. The nearest alternative is 여기로 가 주세요 ('go to here'), which you use when pointing at a map pin rather than reading out a full street address — 이 주소 names the written address, 여기 points at a spot. The classic English-speaker mistake is dropping the helper verb and saying 이 주소 가요, which sounds like you are narrating your own plan ('I'm going to this address') rather than requesting the driver to take you there; the 주세요 ('do it for me') is what makes it a polite request.

Dropping 주세요 and saying 이 주소 가요 — that's you stating your own plan, not asking the driver; you need 가 주세요 to make it a request to him.
Calling the driver 아저씨 ('mister') to get his attention — it's not rude but sounds rough; 기사님 is the respectful, standard term.

usage: 존댓말 — said while pointing at a map pin or address on your phone
반말 — only to a friend who's driving
Could you take me here, please?
Softer/more formal — when you want to sound extra polite
Natural extension — asking the route to a pin you're showing
examples: 여기로 가 주세요.
Please take me here.
The bare request while tapping a location on the screen
여기로 가 주세요. 지도에 표시해 놨어요.
Please take me here. I've marked it on the map.
표시하다 = to mark; you've pinned the spot in advance
여기로 가 주세요. 큰길 말고 골목 안쪽이에요.
Please take me here. It's not on the main road, it's inside the alley.
Helping the driver who might stop at the wrong, easier spot
nuance: You say this to a driver while physically showing a point — a dropped pin, a photo of a place, a spot on a paper map — customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말, which suits any service stranger. Make it gentler with 가 주시겠어요?; drop to 반말 가 줘 only with a friend at the wheel. The dividing line with 이 주소로 가 주세요 is what you're pointing at: 여기 ('here') points at a location or pin, while 이 주소 names a written street address you read aloud — if you're holding up a map you want 여기, if you're reading numbers you want 이 주소. The English-speaker error is to say 여기 가 주세요 without the 로 particle; while Koreans do drop it casually, the clean, taught form marks the destination with 로/으로, so 여기로 가 주세요. Another trap is using 이리 (a stiff, literary 'this way') instead of the everyday 여기.

mistakes: Using 에서 instead of 로 — 여기에서 means 'from here' (starting point), but you want the destination, so it's 여기로 가 주세요.
Saying 여기 와 주세요 ('please come here') — 오다 (come) is wrong because you're already in the cab going somewhere; the verb is 가다 (go).
Pointing and only saying 여기 — to a driver that's abrupt; add 로 가 주세요 so it's a complete polite request.

usage: 존댓말 — the standard way to tell a driver to pull over
반말 — to a friend driving you
Could you pull over here, please?
Softer — 좀 + 시겠어요 cushions the request
Please stop here for a sec.
Natural extension — 잠깐 implies a brief stop, e.g. to let someone off
examples: 여기서 세워 주세요.
Please stop here.
The bare instruction as you arrive
아, 여기서 세워 주세요. 다 왔어요.
Oh, stop here please. We're here.
아 signals you just recognized the spot
저기 신호등 지나서 바로 여기서 세워 주세요.
Right after that traffic light, please stop here.
Giving the driver a landmark so he slows in time
nuance: This tells the driver to pull over and stop where you are now, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말 (세워 주세요 = 'please make it stop for me'). Soften it with 좀 and 세워 주시겠어요?; the 반말 세워 줘 is for a friend. Note the causative verb: 서다 means 'to stop (oneself)', but you need 세우다 ('to bring to a stop'), because you are asking the driver to stop the car, not asking the car to halt on its own. The nearest alternatives are 저 앞에서 내릴게요 ('I'll get off up ahead'), which announces where you'll exit rather than commanding a stop, and 여기 세워 주세요 without 서 — Koreans say both 여기서 and 여기에서, and 여기서 is the natural contraction. The English-speaker mistake is saying 여기서 서 주세요 with the intransitive 서다, which sounds like you're telling the driver to stand still personally; use the causative 세워 주세요.

english: I'll get off just up ahead.
usage: 존댓말 — politely announcing where you want to be let out
I will get off just ahead.
More formal (격식) — 겠습니다 is crisp and deferential
I'll get off at the crosswalk ahead.
Natural extension — naming the exact landmark
examples: 저 앞에서 내릴게요.
I'll get off up ahead.
The bare announcement pointing forward
저 앞에서 내릴게요. 거기 편의점 앞에요.
I'll get off up ahead, in front of that convenience store there.
Pinpointing with a visible shop
지금 세우긴 좀 그렇고, 저 앞에서 내릴게요.
It's a bit awkward to stop now, so I'll get off just ahead.
Real situation when the current spot is a no-stopping zone
nuance: You say this to tell the driver where you intend to get out, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말. The -ㄹ게요 ending signals your own intention/decision ('I'll go ahead and get off'), which is softer and more natural here than barking a command. The 반말 form is 내릴게; the formal/격식 form 내리겠습니다 suits a very stiff or business-car setting. The dividing line with 여기서 세워 주세요 is who the verb is about: 세워 주세요 commands the driver to stop the car, while 내릴게요 describes your own action of getting off — Koreans often pair them ('저 앞에서 세워 주세요' to command, '저 앞에서 내릴게요' to announce). The English-speaker mistake is translating 'I want to get off' as 내리고 싶어요, which is grammatically fine but sounds like a child stating a desire; the adult, situation-appropriate form is the intention ending 내릴게요. Also note 저 앞 ('that spot ahead, away from us') versus 이 앞 ('right in front of us') — 저 is what you point to a short distance forward.

Saying 이 앞에서 when the spot is some meters ahead — 이 앞 is right at your position; for a point further forward use 저 앞.

usage: 존댓말 — asking the driver the trip time
How long do you think it'll take?
Softer — 걸릴까요 asks for the driver's estimate/opinion
How long does it take from here?
Natural extension — anchoring the question to your current point
examples: 거기까지 얼마나 걸려요?
How long does it take to get there?
까지 = 'up to/to', marking the destination
공항까지 얼마나 걸려요? 비행기 시간이 좀 빠듯해서요.
How long to the airport? My flight time is a bit tight.
Explaining why you're anxious about the time
이 시간에 강남까지 얼마나 걸려요? 차 많이 막혀요?
How long to Gangnam at this hour? Is there a lot of traffic?
Real situation asking about time plus traffic together
nuance: This asks the driver how much time the ride will take, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말. The verb 걸리다 here means 'to take (time)' and is the fixed phrase for durations — 얼마나 걸려요? is THE way to ask 'how long'. Make it tentative with 얼마나 걸릴까요? (inviting a guess); 반말 is 얼마나 걸려? Do not confuse this with 얼마예요? ('how much is it?'), which asks about money — 걸려요 is time, 예요 is price. The English-speaker mistake is mapping 'how long' onto length and saying 얼마나 길어요?, which literally asks about physical length and is wrong for duration; time always pairs with 걸리다. Another trap is 시간 얼마나 있어요?, which asks 'how much time do you have', a totally different meaning. Add the destination with 까지 (e.g. 공항까지 얼마나 걸려요?).

english: Please go a bit faster / Please hurry.
usage: 존댓말 — 좀 softens the push so it isn't bossy
Could you hurry just a little?
More formal/polite — 서둘러 주시겠어요 is gentler and refined
Please go as fast as possible.
Natural extension — 최대한 = 'as much as possible', for real urgency
examples: 좀 빨리 가 주세요.
Please hurry a little.
The bare urgent request — note 좀 keeps it polite
죄송한데 좀 빨리 가 주세요. 시간이 없어서요.
Sorry, but please hurry. I'm short on time.
죄송한데 apologizes in advance for pressing him
기차 시간이 다 돼서요, 좀 빨리 가 주실 수 있을까요?
My train's about to leave, so could you possibly go a bit faster?
Real situation — softening a hurry request with a reason and 수 있을까요
nuance: You say this to urge the driver to speed up, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말, and the little word 좀 ('a bit/please') is essential — without it 빨리 가 주세요 can sound like a curt order. For extra courtesy use 서둘러 주시겠어요? or attach a reason ('시간이 없어서요'); 반말 is 빨리 가 줘. The nearest alternative is 서둘러 주세요 ('please hurry'), which focuses on haste in general, while 빨리 가 주세요 specifically means drive faster — both are fine, but Koreans soften either with 좀. The English-speaker mistake is the bare imperative 빨리 가요 or even 빨리!, which to a stranger is rude; you need 좀 ... 주세요 to make it a polite request, and prefacing with 죄송한데 makes pressing him feel considerate. Be aware drivers can only do so much in traffic, so Koreans frame it as a request, not a demand.

usage: 존댓말 — quick, natural way to ask if cards are accepted
반말 — to a friend, e.g. checking a shared cab
More formal — 결제/가능 is fuller and more polite
Is it okay if I pay by card?
Natural extension — 카드로 names the method explicitly
examples: 카드 돼요?
Can I pay by card?
The bare two-word check before the ride or at the end
현금이 없는데 카드 돼요?
I don't have cash — does card work?
Explaining why you're asking
카드 돼요? 아니면 계좌이체라도 될까요?
Can I pay by card? Or could I even do a bank transfer?
Real situation offering a backup payment method
nuance: This asks whether the taxi takes card payment, customer-to-driver, in casual 존댓말. The verb 되다 here means 'to be possible/to work', so 카드 돼요? literally is 'does card work?' — a very common, idiomatic way to ask if something is accepted. The fuller polite version is 카드 결제 가능할까요?; 반말 is 카드 돼?. The nearest alternative is 카드로 계산해도 돼요? ('may I pay by card?'), which is more explicit but longer — in a quick taxi exchange the short 카드 돼요? is what Koreans actually say. The English-speaker mistake is translating 'can I' as 할 수 있어요 and producing 카드 할 수 있어요?, which sounds like 'am I able to do card' and is unnatural; the idiom uses 되다, not 할 수 있다. Also avoid 카드 받아요? ('do you receive card?') — understandable but the native phrasing is 돼요?.

usage: 존댓말 — politely telling the driver to keep small change
반말 — to a friend or very casual
More formal (격식) — 습니다 is crisp and courteous
Natural extension — explicitly telling him to take it
examples: 잔돈은 괜찮아요.
Keep the change.
The bare phrase as you hand over a bill
9,500원이요? 잔돈은 괜찮아요.
9,500 won? Keep the change.
Rounding up a fare to the nearest bill
감사합니다. 잔돈은 괜찮으니까 그냥 받으세요.
Thank you. Keep the change, please just take it.
Real situation insisting when the driver hesitates
nuance: You say this to let the driver keep the leftover change, customer-to-driver, in 존댓말. 잔돈 = 'change/small money', and 괜찮아요 here means 'it's fine (don't bother returning it)'. The topic particle 은 on 잔돈 nicely sets 'as for the change...'. Formal is 괜찮습니다; 반말 잔돈은 됐어. The nearest alternative is 그냥 가지세요 ('just keep it'), which is more direct, while 잔돈은 괜찮아요 is the softer, indirect way Koreans usually phrase a tip. Note tipping is NOT customary in Korean taxis — this is mainly used to round up a fare or skip tiny coins, not to add a percentage. The English-speaker mistake is inventing a literal 'keep the change' as 변화를 지켜요, mistranslating 'change' as 변화 (transformation) and 'keep' as 지키다 (guard) — the money sense is 잔돈, and you decline it with 괜찮아요. Another error is using 거스름돈 wrongly; 거스름돈 is fine too but 잔돈 is the everyday word.

Marking 잔돈 with 를 (잔돈을 괜찮아요) — 괜찮다 is descriptive and takes 은/는 or no particle here; say 잔돈은 괜찮아요.
Expecting to tip a percentage — Korean taxis don't use tipping; this phrase just rounds the fare up, so don't over-explain a 'tip'.

english: Could you please open the trunk?

Could you open the trunk, please?
짐 좀 실을게요, 트렁크 열어 주세요.
I've got luggage to load, please open the trunk.
Natural extension — explaining you have bags
examples: 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요.
Please open the trunk.
The bare request as you approach with a suitcase
캐리어가 있어서요, 트렁크 좀 열어 주세요.
I have a suitcase, so please open the trunk.
캐리어 = rolling suitcase; giving the reason
기사님, 짐이 좀 많은데 트렁크 좀 열어 주시겠어요?
Driver, I have quite a bit of luggage — could you open the trunk?

usage: 존댓말 — what a driver says to YOU; you may also hear it

More formal (격식) — 착용하다 is the official 'to wear/fasten'

Please put on your seatbelt.

손님, 뒷자리도 안전벨트 매 주세요.
Sir/ma'am, please buckle up in the back seat too.
손님 = 'customer'; drivers must remind back-seat riders by law
출발하겠습니다. 안전벨트 매 주세요.
I'll get going now. Please fasten your seatbelt.

usage: 존댓말 — politely insisting on the metered fare
반말 — only with a friend (you wouldn't really say this to a driver in 반말)
More pointed — 켜고 가다 = turn it on and drive

Natural extension — confirming it's metered before haggling starts

Please turn on the meter.
The bare request if the driver hasn't started it

Please turn on the meter. We go by the meter, right?

저, 미터기 켜 주세요. 정찰제 아니고 미터기로요.

usage: How much is the base fare?
May I ask the base fare?
Softer/more formal — 인가요 is gentle and polite
How much more on top of the base fare?
Natural extension — asking the extra beyond the base
examples: 기본요금이 얼마예요?
How much is the base fare?
The bare question about the starting fare
여기 택시 기본요금이 얼마예요?
What's the taxi base fare here?
Asking because it differs by city/region
심야에는 기본요금이 얼마예요? 할증 붙죠?
What's the base fare late at night? There's a surcharge, right?

('how much is it?'). The subject particle 이 ('기본요금이') is correct because 기본요금 is the thing being asked about; softer is 얼마인가요?, 반말 is 얼마야?. english: Please don't take a detour (the long way).
usage: Please don't go the long way.
존댓말 — politely asking not to detour for a higher fare
Could you please not take a detour?
Natural positive extension — asking for the direct route instead
examples: 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
Please don't take the long way.
The bare polite request not to detour
여기 길 잘 아니까 돌아가지 말아 주세요.
I know this area well, so please don't go the long way.
Signaling you'll notice a detour, said gently
내비대로만 가 주세요. 돌아가지 말고요.
Please just follow the GPS, and don't take a detour.
Real situation asking him to stick to the navigation route

usage: 존댓말 — said by you or the driver as you reach the spot
More formal (격식) — a driver may announce it this way
Natural extension — 거의 = 'almost', when not quite there yet
examples: 다 왔어요. 여기서 세워 주세요.
We're here. Please stop here.
Pairing arrival with the stop request
손님, 다 왔습니다. 14,200원입니다.
Sir/ma'am, we've arrived. That'll be 14,200 won.
How a driver announces arrival and the fare
다 왔어요. 저기 건물 앞에 잠깐 세워 주시면 돼요.
We're here. You can just pull up in front of that building.
Real situation directing the final stop on arrival

The English-speaker mistake is using the present 와요 or saying 다 가요 — arrival is expressed with the past 왔어요 (the coming is completed), and the verb is 오다 here, not 가다. Another trap is treating it as literally 'all came' for people; it's an idiom for 'we've arrived'.

english: Thank you, take care / keep up the good work.
usage: 존댓말 — the standard goodbye to a driver as you leave
반말 — to a friend (rarely to a driver)
More formal (격식) — 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges the completed effort
Natural extension — a warm alternative sign-off
examples: 감사합니다, 수고하세요.
Thank you, take care.
The bare parting line as you step out
잘 왔습니다. 감사합니다, 수고하세요.
Got here well. Thank you, take care.
Adding 'we arrived fine' before the goodbye
카드 결제됐어요? 네, 감사합니다. 수고하세요!
Did the card go through? Yes, thank you. Take care!
Real situation closing out the payment then leaving

The completed-action formal version 수고하셨습니다 ('you've worked hard') is said when THEY finish for you; while you leave mid-shift, 수고하세요 (ongoing) is the right pick. A warm alternative is 안전 운전하세요 ('drive safe'). The key cultural/English-speaker mistake is saying 수고하세요 to someone OF HIGHER STATUS (a boss, a much older person, a professor) — it can sound condescending, as if praising their effort from above; with a driver it's perfectly normal, but never say it to your superior. Also, don't translate 'take care' as 조심하세요 ('be careful'), which warns of danger rather than thanking effort.

english: Could you call me a taxi, please?
usage: 존댓말 — to a hotel/restaurant staff member
Could you call a taxi for me?
More formal — 한 대 ('one [vehicle]') + 시겠어요 is polished
Natural extension — 잡다 = flag one down on the street
examples: 택시 좀 불러 주세요.
Please call a taxi for me.

죄송한데 택시 좀 불러 주세요. 비가 와서요.
Sorry, could you call me a taxi? It's raining.

I'm checking out — could you call a taxi to the airport?

Another trap is omitting 좀, which makes the request feel curt.

More formal is 택시 한 대 불러 주시겠어요?; 반말 is 불러 줘. Another trap is omitting 좀, which makes the request feel curt.
The nearest alternative is 택시 잡아 주세요, where 잡다 ('to catch/grab') means flagging one down on the street — the dividing line is method: 부르다 = phone/app a cab to come, 잡다 = hail a passing one.
The English-speaker mistake is translating 'call' as 전화하다 and saying 택시한테 전화해 주세요 ('please phone to the taxi'), which is odd because you summon the service, not ring a specific cab; the verb is 부르다.

mistakes: Saying 택시한테 전화해 주세요 — you summon a cab with 부르다, not 전화하다; say 택시 좀 불러 주세요.
Confusing 부르다 and 잡다 — 부르다 is call/summon (by phone/app), 잡다 is hail on the street; pick by method.
Dropping 좀 — without the softener 택시 불러 주세요 sounds abrupt; add 좀: 택시 좀 불러 주세요.

english: Driver, how do we get here?
usage: Driver, how do we get there?
존댓말 — asking the route while showing a destination
Do you know how to get here?
Softer/indirect — 가는지 아세요 checks his knowledge politely
여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요.
Please tell me the way to get here.
Natural extension — directly asking for directions
examples: 기사님, 여기 어떻게 가요?
Driver, how do we get here?
The bare route question, showing your phone
여기 어떻게 가요? 골목이 복잡해서 잘 모르겠어요.
How do we get here? The alleys are confusing and I'm not sure.
Admitting you don't know the maze of streets
여기 어떻게 가요? 빠른 길로 가면 좋겠는데요.
How do we get here? I'd prefer the quickest route.
Real situation asking for the route and hinting at the fast one
nuance: You ask this to a driver about the route to a place you're showing, customer-to-driver, in plain 존댓말, often opening with 기사님 to address him respectfully. 어떻게 = 'how', 가요 = 'do (we) go', so 여기 어떻게 가요? = 'how do we get here?'. A softer, indirect version is 여기 어떻게 가는지 아세요? ('do you know how to get here?'); 반말 is 여기 어떻게 가?. The nearest alternative is 여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 ('please tell me the way'), which directly requests directions, whereas 어떻게 가요? asks the method more openly — both are natural. The English-speaker mistake is calquing 'how can I get there' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요?, which over-uses the ability form and sounds stilted; Koreans simply say 어떻게 가요? Another error is 어디 가요? ('where are we going?'), which asks the destination, not the route.

A softer, indirect version is 여기 어떻게 가는지 아세요? ('do you know how to get here?'); 반말 is 여기 어떻게 가?.

The nearest alternative is 여기 가는 길 좀 알려 주세요 ('please tell me the way'), which directly requests directions, whereas 어떻게 가요? asks the method more openly — both are natural. Another contrast is 어디 가요? ('where are we going?'), which asks the destination, not the route.
The English-speaker mistake is calquing 'how can I get there' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요?, which over-uses the ability form and sounds stilted; Koreans simply say 어떻게 가요?.

mistakes: Saying 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? — the ability form is unneeded; the natural route question is just 어떻게 가요?.
Confusing 어떻게 (how) with 어디 (where) — 어디 가요? asks the destination; for the route use 어떻게 가요?.
Using 오다 (여기 어떻게 와요) when you mean traveling there — for going to the spot use 가다: 여기 어떻게 가요?.
